analysis.one_liner: Caps prices of federally funded drugs and cancels exclusivity for overcharging.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Health Committee without a hearing or a vote, having gained one Republican cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Drug makers who keep patents on discoveries financed by federal research grants — a share of nearly every new drug — would face price rules: they must report their costs and pricing, set launch prices the second year at or below a government-determined 'reasonable' level, and limit later increases to the rise in prescription drug prices generally. Manufacturers that overcharge could lose their market exclusivity, face fines up to $1 million per day, and be barred from future federal licensing deals; NIH-funded patents that skip the government's new disclosure rules could be canceled in court. The bill never got a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors on Medicare, patients paying out of pocket under high-deductible plans, and Medicaid programs — anyone whose costs are pegged to drug list prices. Also taxpayers, who fund NIH research but pay premium prices for the resulting drugs; penalty payments would be transferred to NIH.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare patients and taxpayers funding NIH

how_it_helps.text: Caps the list price of drugs built on federally supported patents at the committee's reasonable-price determination starting the second year on the market, and limits later increases to the rise in the prescription-drug price index [S2, S3].
Requires manufacturers to reveal R&D spending, federal funding claimed through tax breaks, and marketing budgets, so pricing decisions can be audited against public contributions [S3].

Penalties for overcharging include immediate loss of market exclusivity — opening the drug to generic competition — plus civil fines up to $1 million per day, with collections transferred to NIH [S3].
Creates a private right of action to cancel patents that failed to disclose the federal grants behind the invention, closing a loophole in existing Bayh-Dole disclosure rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers holding patents on NIH-supported inventions — an estimated broad share of new drugs, since an analysis cited in the bill found NIH funding contributed directly or indirectly to all 210 new molecular entities approved 2010–2016 — who would face price caps, fines, and loss of exclusivity for overcharging.

drawbacks.text: Defining a 'reasonable' price is genuinely hard: the bill delegates it to a new private nonprofit committee applying a yet-to-be-developed National Academy of Medicine methodology, which could misprice drugs and dampen investment in future medicines.

The bill only covers drugs tied to patents where the sponsor kept title to federally funded inventions or entered licensing agreements after enactment — so pricing leverage depends on how narrowly the 'applicable drug' pool is drawn in practice.
Manufacturers facing loss of exclusivity could be pushed to shift launches abroad or restructure deals to avoid coverage, and enforcement through patent cancellation invites years of litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public upside is large: taxpayers effectively fund the early science behind most new drugs and then pay premium prices for the results, and this bill attaches real price conditions and penalties to that arrangement. The main risk is execution — a price-setting committee with a vague methodology could produce arbitrary determinations, and the industry would fight through every legal channel. As drafted, the affordability gains outweigh the design risks.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in July 2019, referred to the Senate HELP Committee, and left there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote through the end of the 116th Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. Van Hollen introduced S. 2387 on July 31, 2019, joined by Sen. Tim Scott of Florida, giving the drug-pricing bill a bipartisan pair of sponsors [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day, which is the last recorded action in its history [S1, S5].
It drew a single Republican cosponsor and no further movement before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S4, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers holding patents on federally funded inventions: they keep full pricing power over drugs built partly at public expense, with no committee review, price caps, or disclosure requirements ever taking effect. Medicare beneficiaries and other patients paying list-price-linked costs get nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug manufacturers keeping pricing power

for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsor, making the bill bipartisan at introduction

against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on S. 2387 — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the 116th Congress

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought S. 2387 to the Senate floor; the bill never got a floor vote in two and a half years

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Opposed government price-setting for patented drugs during the 116th Congress, when the industry spent record sums lobbying against multiple drug-pricing measures

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan at introduction — a Democrat sponsor with one Republican cosponsor — but opposition is harder to read: no vote ever occurred, and the committee with the power to move it was chaired by a Republican who never acted on it.

industries.note: Drugs built on NIH-supported patents would face a government-set reasonable price cap, mandatory cost disclosure, fines up to $1 million per day, and loss of market exclusivity for overcharging. The industry's pricing power on publicly funded inventions is directly at stake, and it gains from the bill dying.
Taxpayers fund the research that produces these drugs; the bill would return penalty collections to NIH and require disclosure of federal grants in drug patent applications [S3].

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug wholesalers
industries.note: Their fees are calculated as a percentage of drug list prices, so lower reasonable prices would shrink their per-unit revenue, though a more transparent pricing structure could simplify their market [S3].
